fullPassage: At a rich merchant's house, there was a birthday party for the merchant's son, and the children of rich and great people were there. Among them was a handsome boy, the son of the editor of a newspaper. He said, "My dad can put everybody's dad in the newspaper. People are afraid of him, my mom says, because he can do whatever he wants with the paper." "But my dad can buy a hundred dollars' worth of candy, and give it to children. Can your dad do that?" asked the merchant's son. "And those whose names end in 'sen' can never be anything at all," he continued. The editor's son was very angry at what he had said, for his father's name was Petersen. But outside the door was a poor boy. His status was so low that he was not even allowed to enter the room. The boy was there to help with the party, and the merchant's son told him to stand behind the door and wait for his call. There he stood, watching the well-dressed children having such a good time inside. "Oh, if I could be one of them," he thought. Then he heard what the merchant's son said about names, and what he said was enough to make him even more unhappy. His parents back home did not even have a penny to buy a newspaper, and worse, his father's name, and of course his own, ended in "sen." But he was born into the world, and the station of life was chosen for him, so he had to be satisfied. And this is what happened that night. Many years passed, and the children grew up. There stood a splendid house in the town. It was much bigger and fancier than the one where the merchant's son had had his birthday party long ago. Which of the children we talked about could say this house was his own? The house belonged to the poor little boy who had stood behind the door that night. He really had become something great, although his name ended in "sen."

부유한 집에서 자란 아이들은 항상 행복하다.

questions.passage: At a rich merchant's house, there was a birthday party for the merchant's son, and the children of rich and great people were there. Among them was a handsome boy, the son of the editor of a newspaper. He said, "My dad can put everybody's dad in the newspaper. People are afraid of him, my mom says, because he can do whatever he wants with the paper." "But my dad can buy a hundred dollars' worth of candy, and give it to children. Can your dad do that?" asked the merchant's son. "And those whose names end in 'sen' can never be anything at all," he continued. The editor's son was very angry at what he had said, for his father's name was Petersen. But outside the door was a poor boy. His status was so low that __________. The boy was there to help with the party, and the merchant's son told him to stand behind the door and wait for his call. There he stood, watching the well-dressed children having such a good time inside. "Oh, if I could be one of them," he thought. Then he heard what the merchant's son said about names, and what he said was enough to make him even more unhappy. His parents back home did not even have a penny to buy a newspaper, and worse, his father's name, and of course his own, ended in "sen." But he was born into the world, and the station of life was chosen for him, so he had to be satisfied. And this is what happened that night. Many years passed, and the children grew up. There stood a splendid house in the town. It was much bigger and fancier than the one where the merchant's son had had his birthday party long ago. Which of the children we talked about could say this house was his own? The house belonged to the poor little boy who had stood behind the door that night. He really had become something great, although his name ended in "sen."

det.korean: he was not even allowed(그는 ~조차 허락되지 않았다) to enter the room(방에 들어가는 것)
det.analysis:
구문 분석: he(주어) + was not even allowed(수동태 be allowed to의 부정: ~하는 것조차 허락되지 않았다) + to enter the room(들어가는 것). be allowed to + 동사원형 = ~하도록 허락되다.

단어 순서: he → was → not → even → allowed → to → enter → the → room (9단어).
det.tip: be allowed to + 동사원형 = ~하도록 허락되다. not even=~조차 (아닌). 낮은 신분을 강조.
